claims.claim: Closed-loop community-health-worker (CHW) → nurse → provider referral coordination (three-tier care coordination with every referral tracked to completion, as run by Mi Salud in rural Washington) is nationally applicable in the USA.

rationale.label: (a) Supported by national evidence?
rationale.text: [SUPPORTED] CHW interventions have strong national evidence, including randomized trials (IMPaCT: ~$2,500 saved/patient in year 1, 66% of hospital days vs matched controls) and AHRQ's documentation of pay-for-performance closed-loop models. The closed-loop referral concept itself is an established quality-improvement framework (AHRQ care-coordination literature; peer-reviewed work on closed-loop social-care referrals). Evidence specifically combining all three tiers (CHW → nurse → telehealth provider with loop closure) in US rural settings is thinner but the components are each well-evidenced.

rationale.label: (b) Already practiced nationally?
rationale.text: [PARTIALLY] Named programs practice close variants: Pathways Community HUB / PCHI (CHW "pathways" tracked to completion, nationally certified, used in many communities), IMPaCT (evidence-based CHW program), and closed-loop referral platforms (Unite Us, findhelp, NowPow) used by health systems nationwide. However, no widely adopted national program combines CHW identification, nurse screening/onboarding, telehealth provider treatment, and mandatory loop closure back to the CHW as a single integrated, tracked workflow — practice is fragmented across these actors.

rationale.label: (c) Feasible under national policy?
rationale.text: [PARTIALLY] Medicare now reimburses CHW-delivered Community Health Integration services (CPT 98160–98162 / G0019, G0022, G0023, G0024, G0322 as of CY2024 PFS), and CHWs may be employed by a community-based organization under general supervision — so the model's billing skeleton exists nationally. But Medicaid CHW coverage is state-by-state (certification, scope, and payment pathways vary widely per NASHP/KFF), and the $50B CMS Rural Health Transformation Program (awards to all 50 states from 2026, ~$200M average first-year) provides grant, not sustained fee-for-service, funding. Feasibility is real but uneven by state and dependent on braided funding.

rationale.label: (d) Where is the gap? — Mi Salud's integrated loop is the gap
rationale.text:
What is NOT done nationally: (1) systematic tracking of every referral to completion — referral leakage remains high nationally (benchmarks show a large share of referrals never complete); (2) a single accountable workflow spanning CHW identification → nurse screening → telehealth provider → closed-loop return to the CHW — most closed-loop platforms stop at social-service referrals, and most HUB models stop at CHW-to-resource linkage; (3) integrated telehealth provider tier with rural vulnerable-population targeting funded through one coordinated model. This integration is Mi Salud's differentiator; it is nationally applicable in concept but not currently practiced as a unified model nationally.

Key numbers: CHI G0019 national rate ~$80.56/month (60 min), G0022 ~$50.26; IMPaCT RCTs: ~$2,500 saved/patient year 1, 66% of hospital days, 94% NPS; CHW referral completion in community-to-facility literature: 34–97% (median 74%); RHT Program: $50B over 5 years, all 50 states, ~$200M average first-year award.

State Policies for Expanding Medicaid Coverage of CHW Services (KFF)" url: https://www.kff.org/medicaid/state-policies-for-expanding-medicaid-coverage-of-community-health-worker-chw-services/ note: > Medicaid payment for CHW services is authorized in a subset of states and takes differing forms (state plan, waiver, managed-care), confirming significant state variation in feasibility.

Connecting Those at Risk to Care: Quick Start Guide to the Pathways Community HUB Model (AHRQ)" url: https://www.ahrq.gov/sites/default/files/wysiwyg/innovations/CommHub_QuickStart.pdf note: > AHRQ documents the Pathways Community HUB — a nationally certified, pay-for- performance care-coordination model in which CHWs work assigned "pathways" that are closed only when the risk factor is resolved — the closest national analogue to Mi Salud's tracked-to-completion loop.

Pathways Community HUB Model (PCHI)" url: https://www.pchi-hub.org/ note: > The PCHI model operates in numerous US communities using CHWs plus a central HUB to remove social barriers, evidencing that closed-loop CHW coordination is already practiced nationally, though not universally.

Unite Us — Connecting Communities, Data & Care" url: https://uniteus.com/ note: > Unite Us operates closed-loop referral networks nationally, showing the referral- tracking infrastructure component is commercially available at national scale.

Referral Leakage Benchmark Report 2026 (Linear Health)" url: https://linear.health/blog/referral-leakage-benchmark-report-2026 note: > Referral leakage (referred care never completed) remains a large national problem across specialties — the problem Mi Salud's tracked-to-completion loop targets is widespread and largely unsolved in standard practice.

CMS Launches Landmark $50 Billion Rural Health Transformation Program" url: https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/press-releases/cms-launches-landmark-50-billion-rural-health-transformation-program note: > CMS's $50B RHT program (Sept 2025) funds state strategies for rural care-delivery innovation and coordination; ~$200M average first-year awards to all 50 states (announced Dec 29, 2025) create a national financing vehicle for models like this.

Care Coordination — AHRQ" url: https://www.ahrq.gov/ncepcr/research/care-coordination/index.html note: > AHRQ frames deliberate organizing of patient care activities and timely information sharing among participants as a core quality lever, supporting the coordination concept but without mandating a specific three-tier staffing model.

claims.claim: Multimodal, native-language patient intake (voice, SMS, text, handwritten notes — in the patient's language) is nationally applicable for US rural healthcare access.
claims.summary: Overall verdict: **PARTIALLY SUPPORTED**. The evidence strongly supports the need for language- and modality-flexible intake in rural care, and federal policy already requires meaningful language access for LEP patients. What is missing is a widely deployed, end-to-end national standard or reimbursement pathway for multimodal intake across voice, SMS, text, paper/handwritten capture, and patient-preferred language.

rationale.label: (a) Does evidence show language/modality barriers block rural care access?
rationale.text:
[SUPPORTED] National evidence shows LEP is associated with worse access to care, less preventive care, and more difficulty obtaining a usual source of care. Rural access literature also explicitly names limited English fluency and low health literacy as barriers to timely care, and rural health-literacy work shows plain-language and telephone outreach can improve screening participation. Taken together, the evidence supports the premise that multimodal, native-language intake is addressing a real rural access barrier rather than a niche convenience.

Strongest sources:
1. Access to Care Among Adults with Limited English Proficiency — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9971409/
2. Healthcare Access in Rural Communities Overview - Rural Health Information Hub — https://www.ruralhealthinfo.org/topics/healthcare-access
3. Health Literacy Research in Rural Areas — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8590389/

rationale.label: (b) Are there existing national programs/products doing this?
rationale.text:
[PARTIALLY SUPPORTED] There are clear national policy frameworks and a growing product ecosystem, but the market is still fragmented. HHS/CMS policy requires language access and telehealth guidance contemplates non-English-speaking patients, while national platforms like CareMessage support bidirectional multilingual texting and vendors such as Sunoh.ai advertise multilingual voice-based documentation. However, the evidence base points more to point solutions and partial workflows than to a standardized national multimodal intake stack that works across modalities and rural settings.

Strongest sources:
1. Section 1557: Ensuring Meaningful Access for Individuals with Limited English Proficiency | HHS.gov — https://www.hhs.gov/civil-rights/for-individuals/section-1557/fs-limited-english-proficiency/index.html
2. TELEHEALTH FOR PROVIDERS: WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW — https://www.cms.gov/files/document/telehealth-toolkit-providers.pdf
3. Using Bi-Directional Text Messaging to Engage Patients | CareMessage — https://www.caremessage.org/using-bi-directional-text-messaging-to-engage-patients/

rationale.label: (c) Do policies/mandates support it?
rationale.text:
[SUPPORTED] Section 1557, CLAS, Title VI/Section 504-linked Medicaid language access obligations, and CMS/CHIPRA reimbursement pathways all support language access and translation/interpretation services. The policy direction is clear: covered entities must provide meaningful access, plain-language information, notices in top languages, and no-cost language assistance; Medicaid states may reimburse interpretation costs and can claim enhanced match in some cases. These policies do not mandate the exact multimodal intake architecture Mi Salud uses, but they do strongly support the underlying practice.

Strongest sources:
1. Translation and Interpretation Services | Medicaid — https://www.medicaid.gov/medicaid/financial-management/medicaid-administrative-claiming/translation-and-interpretation-services
2. CLAS Standards - Think Cultural Health — https://thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/clas/standards
3. Enrollment and Access Barriers for People with Limited English Proficiency — https://www.macpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/Enrollment-and-Access-Barriers-for-People-with-Limited-English-Proficiency.pdf

rationale.label: (d) What is the national gap?
rationale.text:
[SUPPORTED] The gap is not whether language access is needed; it is that rural health systems lack a broadly adopted, reimbursed, interoperable multimodal intake pathway in the patient’s language. MACPAC and CMS describe language access obligations and reimbursement options, but implementation varies by state and provider, and rural broadband/workforce constraints make video-only or portal-only approaches brittle. Nationally, the market offers pieces of the workflow—texting, interpretation, multilingual documentation—but not a universal, low-bandwidth, low-literacy, language-concordant intake standard.

Strongest sources:
1. Enrollment and Access Barriers for People with Limited English Proficiency — https://www.macpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/Enrollment-and-Access-Barriers-for-People-with-Limited-English-Proficiency.pdf
2. TELEHEALTH FOR PROVIDERS: WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW — https://www.cms.gov/files/document/telehealth-toolkit-providers.pdf
3. Healthcare Access in Rural Communities Overview - Rural Health Information Hub — https://www.ruralhealthinfo.org/topics/healthcare-access

claims.claim: BYOD (bring-your-own-device) remote patient monitoring is nationally applicable for U.S. rural populations.
claims.summary: BYOD RPM is nationally feasible and increasingly practical, but it is not uniformly universal across rural America. The policy and vendor stack is real: Medicare reimburses RPM/RTM, HHS recognizes asynchronous/store-and-forward telehealth, and vendors already ship cellular or app-based RPM workflows nationally. The limiting factors are access, not concept: smartphone ownership is high but not universal, seniors lag, rural broadband is still weaker than suburban access, and some rural patients will need cellular gateways or store-and-forward workflows rather than app-only designs.

rationale.label: (a) Smartphone / smartwatch ownership, including rural and seniors
rationale.text:
[PARTIALLY SUPPORTED] **Rationale:** Pew shows the device base is large enough to make BYOD RPM workable nationally: 91% of U.S. adults own smartphones, and 37% own smartwatches. But adoption drops for older adults (78% smartphone ownership and 24% smartwatch ownership for age 65+), and Pew continues to note that rural adults are less likely than urban adults to own smartphones and less likely than suburban adults to have home broadband. So the demographic base is strong, but BYOD cannot assume every rural or older patient already has the needed device stack.

**3 strongest sources:**
1. Pew mobile fact sheet — 91% smartphone ownership; 78% among adults 65+
2. Pew 2024 mobile technology/home broadband report — rural broadband and smartphone-dependent gaps
3. Pew smartwatch charts — 37% overall; 24% for age 65+

rationale.label: (b) National RPM reimbursement landscape
rationale.text:
[SUPPORTED] **Rationale:** CMS clearly covers remote patient monitoring in Medicare and breaks it into setup, device supply, and treatment-management components. CMS also states the same payment logic applies regardless of the specific device type, and the agency’s MLN guidance ties RPM/RTM to secure electronic transmission, consent, and day-count rules. RTM is also a standing Medicare code family, so nationally there is a reimbursement pathway for both physiologic RPM and therapeutic monitoring.

**3 strongest sources:**
1. CMS Remote Patient Monitoring page — Medicare broadly covers RPM and defines the core components
2. CMS MLN901705 booklet — patient consent, secure upload, and billing rules
3. CMS manual/system documents — RTM codes 98975/98976/98977/98980/98981

rationale.label: (c) Existing BYOD-compatible RPM platforms and home diagnostic kits nationally
rationale.text:
[SUPPORTED] **Rationale:** There are already national vendors built for low-friction monitoring. Tenovi is the clearest example: its cellular gateway works with 60+ FDA-cleared devices, needs no app or Wi-Fi, and pushes data over cellular networks. Optimize Health and Healthie also show the broader national platform layer: software plus patient-friendly devices/support, and support for wearable/mobile-app/home-device workflows. That means BYOD-compatible RPM is not hypothetical; it is already a commercial category.

**3 strongest sources:**
1. Tenovi Gateway page — 60+ devices, no app, no Wi-Fi, cellular transmission
2. Optimize Health remote healthcare page — RPM software with patient-friendly devices and support
3. Healthie remote monitoring glossary — wearable devices, mobile apps, and home-based monitoring devices

rationale.label: (d) Broadband constraints in rural U.S. and store-and-forward as a solution
rationale.text:
[PARTIALLY SUPPORTED] **Rationale:** Rural connectivity is a real constraint. Pew reports rural adults trail suburban adults on home broadband, and FCC’s 2024 broadband reporting shows the federal benchmark gap is still meaningful in rural areas. Store-and-forward is a recognized telehealth modality: HHS explicitly defines asynchronous telehealth as store-and-forward and lists text, images, and report uploads as valid workflows. However, it is only a partial solution for RPM because Medicare’s normal telehealth rules are still largely synchronous, and CMS’s explicit store-and-forward billing example is narrow (G2010, largely tied to specific circumstances rather than a universal RPM workaround).

**3 strongest sources:**
1. FCC Internet Access Services: Status as of June 30, 2024 — national broadband baseline
2. HHS asynchronous telehealth guide — store-and-forward recognized as a telehealth modality
3. CMS telemedicine fact sheet — G2010 store-and-forward is recognized but limited

rationale.label: (e) The national gap
rationale.text:
[SUPPORTED] **Rationale:** The gap is not whether RPM exists nationally; it does. The gap is that universal national applicability requires design choices to bridge uneven device ownership, older-adult adoption, and rural broadband constraints. That is exactly where BYOD plus cellular gateways plus store-and-forward can fill the need: it reduces hardware procurement burden and makes deployment possible in lower-bandwidth communities. The remaining gap is operational, not conceptual—patient onboarding, data transport, and reimbursement alignment still need to be configured to local access realities.

**3 strongest sources:**
1. Pew smartphone and broadband reports — high overall adoption but rural/older gaps remain
2. CMS RPM/RTM guidance — reimbursement is available, but only under defined rules
3. Tenovi / Healthie / Optimize Health — the market already supports low-friction and BYOD-friendly workflows
